An excellent post by EFF on the dangers DRM poses to the open web.

TL;DR: If web DRM (Encrypted Media Extensions) becomes widespread enough to cripple browsers that don't support it, the barrier of entry to bringing a new browser to the market will be insurmountable. Even Firefox forks like Tor Browser and Pale Moon will die, leaving us entirely at Google's and Mozilla's mercy, who have every financial motivation to destroy our experience by locking down the browser to prevent ad blocking, among other nasty things.

With every dollar you spend on a service that requires EME DRM (like Netflix), you're digging your own grave as a consumer and destroying the open Internet.
Why you should boycott Netflix, and any other service that uses web DRM

Sounds like it would be in the best interests of those browsers to support it.

What should content owners to protect their stuff in lieu of DRM?
If they really need DRM, native apps or browser plugins are the way to go. A Netflix app can have all the DRM it wants without "infecting" web standards with non-free components.

As a content owner, this does not work. Plugins don't "just work" putting a barrier between people and my stuff. Apps IMO are too costly to have and maintain on all the platforms you would need to. A standard, even a non free one, is better than appifying the web and relying on plugins that can be hacked easier.

Remember, at the end of the day, it's someone's hard work you want to access, and they have the right to be protected from theft.

Oh, dear. Where do I begin?

The additional cost isn't that much. It's effectively just one more app to maintain, since the browser-based Netflix is itself an app, so you'd just have to replace that one app with two (one for Windows and one for OSX/Linux); they will even share most of their code. Note that this is one more app when you're already maintaining 5 or so (browser-based Netflix, Netflix for Android, IOS, smart TVs etc.).

A non-free standard is not a standard. Putting DRM in a standard undermines the very point of standardization. Standards are meant to provide interoperability. By requiring a proprietary video decoding component that can't be included in a browser without special arrangements with content owners, and then requiring that the hardware support HDCP, you're destroying that interoperability.

As for piracy, I don't believe you need DRM to keep it under control. If you provide a quality service that respects its consumers, people will pay. Look at the video game industry, where intrusive DRM is long dead. Besides, 95% of Netflix viewers are not tech-savvy enough to "rip" a video from a website even if it's streamed in the simplest HTML5 player with zero protection, and the truly determined pirates will break or bypass any DRM anyway – even if technical attempts to break the protection fail, eventually someone with ties to the content owners will leak the source material.

So supporting win32 winUWP, OSX, iOS, iOSTV, Linux of several flavors, Amazon, Roku, TV's embedded Os'es, Android and Android "TV" is not that much harder than a singular standard that can be baked into any browser?
